Learning Objectives

By the end of this lecture, students should be able to: define a network formally; distinguish network types; articulate the intelligence value of network analysis; and identify key analytical questions networks can answer.

Part I: Conceptual Foundations

What Is a Network?

Formal Definition

A network (or graph) is a set of entities (nodes/vertices) connected by relationships (edges/links). Formally: \(G = (V, E)\) where \(V\) is the vertex set and \(E \subseteq V \times V\) is the edge set.


Why this formalism matters:

  • The same mathematical structure underlies any relational system
  • Terrorist cells, power grids, financial flows, and social media all reduce to nodes and edges
  • Shared formalism means shared analytical tools across domains
  • Quantitative rigor reduces analyst bias in pattern recognition


Networks are not merely visualizations — they are structures that encode relationships. Visualization is one output; analysis is the goal.

\(V = \{A, B, C, D, E\}\)

\(|V| = 5\) nodes, \(|E| = 6\) edges

Node B has degree 4 (most connected)

A Brief History of Network Science

Mathematical Origins

  • 1736 — Euler’s Königsberg Bridge Problem: First formal graph theory problem; demonstrated that an Eulerian path requires nodes of even degree.1

  • 1930s–60s — Sociometry: Moreno’s sociograms mapped interpersonal relationships; first systematic social network visualization.2

  • 1960s — Random Graph Theory: Erdős and Rényi established probability models for graph formation; foundational for understanding network connectivity.3

Modern Network Science

  • 1967 — Small World Experiment: Milgram demonstrated six degrees of separation; empirical validation of short path lengths in social networks.4

  • 1998 — Small-World Networks: Watts and Strogatz formalized the clustering/path-length tradeoff that characterizes most real-world networks.5

  • 1999 — Scale-Free Networks: Barabási and Albert identified preferential attachment and power-law degree distributions in real networks.6

  • 2001 — Intelligence Application: Krebs mapped the 9/11 hijacker network, bringing SNA to national security discourse.7

  1. Leonhard Euler, “Solutio problematis ad geometriam situs pertinentis,” Commentarii Academiae Scientiarum Petropolitanae 8 (1741): 128–140.

  2. Jacob L. Moreno, Who Shall Survive? Foundations of Sociometry, Group Psychotherapy and Sociodrama (Washington, D.C.: Nervous and Mental Disease Publishing, 1934).

  3. Paul Erdős and Alfréd Rényi, “On the Evolution of Random Graphs,” Publications of the Mathematical Institute of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences 5 (1960): 17–61.

  4. Stanley Milgram, “The Small World Problem,” Psychology Today 2, no. 1 (1967): 60–67.

  5. Duncan J. Watts and Steven H. Strogatz, “Collective Dynamics of ‘Small-World’ Networks,” Nature 393, no. 6684 (1998): 440–442.

  6. Albert-László Barabási and Réka Albert, “Emergence of Scaling in Random Networks,” Science 286, no. 5439 (1999): 509–512.

  7. Valdis Krebs, “Mapping Networks of Terrorist Cells,” Connections 24, no. 3 (2002): 43–52.

Core Vocabulary: Nodes and Edges

Nodes (Vertices)

  • Represent entities in the network
  • Can be: persons, organizations, locations, events, accounts, documents, states
  • Nodes carry attributes: demographics, role, capacity, status
  • Node count \(= |V|\); also called order of the graph


Edges (Links, Ties)

  • Represent relationships between nodes
  • Can be: communication, transaction, membership, trust, kinship, co-occurrence
  • Edge count \(= |E|\); also called size of the graph
  • Edges carry attributes: weight, direction, timestamp, type

Edge Attribute Examples in Intelligence Contexts

Attribute Type Intel Example
Weight Numeric Call frequency
Direction Boolean Wire transfer flow
Timestamp Temporal Meeting date
Type Categorical Kinship vs. financial
Confidence Ordinal Source reliability
Duration Temporal Relationship length


Analyst Note

Attribute quality drives analytical quality. A network with poorly coded edge types or missing weights produces misleading centrality scores.

Graph Types and Directionality

By Edge Direction

  • Undirected: edges have no directionality; relationship is symmetric (e.g., co-membership in an organization)
  • Directed (digraph): edges have a source and a target; relationship is asymmetric (e.g., wire transfers, command authority)
  • Mixed: some edges directed, some not


By Edge Multiplicity

  • Simple graph: at most one edge between any pair of nodes; no self-loops
  • Multigraph: multiple edges allowed between same pair (e.g., both a phone call and a financial transaction)
  • Pseudograph: self-loops permitted (e.g., a transaction back to the originating account)

By Edge Weight

  • Unweighted: presence/absence only; all edges treated equally
  • Weighted: numeric value on each edge encoding magnitude (frequency, volume, strength)


By Node Type

  • Unipartite (one-mode): all nodes are the same type (e.g., all persons)
  • Bipartite (two-mode): two distinct node types; edges only between types (e.g., persons and events they attended)1
  • Multipartite / Multilayer: multiple node types or multiple relationship layers

  1. Stanley Wasserman and Katherine Faust, Social Network Analysis: Methods and Applications (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1994), 29–35.

Network Density and Sparsity

Density measures how many edges exist relative to the maximum possible:

\[\Delta = \frac{|E|}{|V|(|V|-1)/2} \quad \text{(undirected)}\]

\[\Delta = \frac{|E|}{|V|(|V|-1)} \quad \text{(directed)}\]

  • \(\Delta = 1.0\): complete graph (every node connected to every other)
  • \(\Delta = 0.0\): empty graph (no edges)
  • Most real-world networks are sparse: \(\Delta \ll 0.1\)


Intelligence implications of density:

  • Dense networks: high redundancy, harder to disrupt, strong group cohesion
  • Sparse networks: rely on key connectors (high betweenness); vulnerable to targeted removal
  • Compartmentalized illicit networks are deliberately sparse for operational security1

Worked Example

A network with \(|V| = 10\) nodes and \(|E| = 12\) edges (undirected):

\[\Delta = \frac{12}{10 \cdot 9 / 2} = \frac{12}{45} \approx 0.267\]

Interpretation: about 27% of all possible connections exist. Moderately sparse. Compare: the 9/11 hijacker network had density \(\approx 0.16\).2


Key Point

Density alone does not identify which connections matter — centrality measures do that.

  1. Jorg Raab and H. Brinton Milward, “Dark Networks as Problems,” Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory 13, no. 4 (2003): 413–439.

  2. Krebs, “Mapping Networks of Terrorist Cells,” 45.

Part II: Networks in the Real World

A Typology of Networks

Social Networks

  • Nodes: individuals or groups
  • Edges: communication, friendship, trust, kinship, co-membership
  • Examples: phone call graphs, organizational charts, diaspora networks
  • Analytically relevant to: insider threat, radicalization, influence operations


Organizational Networks

  • Nodes: units, roles, or individuals within institutions
  • Edges: reporting relationships, resource flows, coordination ties
  • Examples: military command structures, terrorist cell hierarchies, NGO coordination
  • Analytically relevant to: leadership targeting, command disruption, resilience assessment

Infrastructure Networks

  • Nodes: physical assets (substations, pipelines, ports, routers)
  • Edges: physical connectivity, flow capacity
  • Examples: power grids, transportation networks, internet topology
  • Analytically relevant to: critical node identification, attack/failure modeling


Information Networks

  • Nodes: accounts, content, platforms
  • Edges: follows, retweets, hyperlinks, citations
  • Examples: social media influence graphs, citation networks, propaganda amplification chains
  • Analytically relevant to: influence operations, disinformation attribution, narrative mapping

Financial and Transaction Networks

Structure

  • Typically bipartite or directed weighted graphs: persons/entities \(\leftrightarrow\) accounts/institutions
  • Edge weight = transaction volume; edge direction = flow direction
  • Temporal dimension critical: layering, placement, and integration in money laundering occur in sequence


Analytical Goals

  • Trace illicit funds across jurisdictions and shell entities
  • Identify structuring patterns (transactions just below reporting thresholds)
  • Detect anomalous flows inconsistent with declared business activity
  • Map financial controllers vs. operational actors (often different nodes)
  • Identify chokepoints for sanctions enforcement

Case: Hawala Networks

Informal value transfer systems (hawala) operate as sparse, trust-based networks connecting brokers (hawaladars) across jurisdictions. No physical currency crosses borders. Network analysis identifies: broker communities, geographic reach, settlement patterns, and high-betweenness brokers who connect otherwise separate regional clusters.1


Key data sources: FinCEN SARs, SWIFT transaction data, corporate registry filings, beneficial ownership databases

  1. Patrick Jost and Harjit Singh Sandhu, “The Hawala Alternative Remittance System and Its Role in Money Laundering,” Interpol General Secretariat (2000).

Dark Networks: Illicit and Covert Systems

Defining Dark Networks

Dark networks are clandestine, trust-based networks that operate outside legal or institutional frameworks. They include terrorist organizations, drug trafficking networks, proliferation supply chains, and criminal enterprises.1


Distinctive Properties

  • Operational security constraints: Actors deliberately limit connectivity to reduce exposure; result is sparse, compartmentalized structure
  • Secrecy-efficiency tradeoff: More connected networks are more efficient but more vulnerable to infiltration and decapitation2
  • Trust substitutes for formal structure: Kinship, ethnicity, and shared criminal history replace bureaucratic coordination
  • Adaptive reorganization: Networks restructure after disruption; static analysis understates resilience

The Secrecy-Efficiency Tradeoff

  • Highly connected cells coordinate well but one arrested member can expose many
  • Highly compartmentalized cells are hard to infiltrate but cannot coordinate complex operations
  • Most sophisticated networks modularize: dense internal clusters, sparse inter-cluster bridges
  • Implication: bridge nodes (high betweenness) are highest-value targets for disruption


Empirical Reference

Analysis of 43 terrorist networks found average density of 0.047 — far sparser than equivalent legal organizations.3

  1. Raab and Milward, “Dark Networks as Problems,” 413.

  2. Valdis Krebs, “Uncloaking Terrorist Networks,” First Monday 7, no. 4 (2002).

  3. Kathleen Carley et al., “Destabilizing Networks,” Connections 24, no. 3 (2002): 31–34.

Part III: The Intelligence Lens

Why Network Analysis for Intelligence?

What Traditional Analysis Misses

  • Attribute-focused analysis (who is this person?) misses relational structure (who does this person connect?)
  • Hierarchical org charts miss informal influence and communication patterns
  • Individual-level reporting does not aggregate to systemic vulnerability
  • Human analysts cannot hold large relational datasets in working memory


What Network Analysis Adds

  • Structural discovery: identifies roles not evident from individual profiles (gatekeepers, brokers, isolates)
  • Comparative assessment: compare network states over time or across cases
  • Targeting prioritization: rank nodes by structural criticality, not just profile prominence
  • Effect prediction: model consequences of node/edge removal before action1

The Analytical Value Proposition

Network analysis transforms intelligence from a collection of facts about entities into a model of relationships — and relationships are where power, influence, vulnerability, and intent live.


Domains where this is established practice:

  • Counterterrorism: cell mapping, leadership targeting
  • Counternarcotics: trafficking route and financial flow analysis
  • Counterproliferation: supplier network mapping
  • Influence operations: amplification network attribution
  • Critical infrastructure protection: vulnerability modeling
  • Financial intelligence: sanctions evasion and money laundering
  • Cyber: threat actor infrastructure mapping

  1. Sean F. Everton, Disrupting Dark Networks (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2012), 10–25.

What Network Analysis Can and Cannot Do

What It Can Do

  • Identify structurally important nodes independent of analyst preconception
  • Detect communities and subgroups within large datasets
  • Track network change over time (growth, contraction, reorganization)
  • Quantify network resilience and vulnerability
  • Generate competing hypotheses about structure and function
  • Integrate multiple data types (financial, communication, geospatial) into a unified model
  • Prioritize collection gaps by identifying structurally important but poorly covered nodes

What It Cannot Do

  • Infer intent from structure alone
  • Compensate for missing data — partial networks can produce misleading centrality scores
  • Establish causation: correlation in network structure does not explain why a relationship exists
  • Replace source validation: garbage in, garbage out
  • Produce finished intelligence without analytical interpretation
  • Resolve questions of identity or attribution without corroborating intelligence


Methodological Warning

Network analysis is a tool, not a conclusion. Structural findings must be interpreted in context, caveated for data incompleteness, and integrated with all-source analysis.1

  1. Nancy Roberts and Sean Everton, “Strategies for Combating Dark Networks,” Journal of Social Structure 12 (2011): 1–32.

Key Analytical Questions Networks Can Answer

Structural Questions

  • Who are the most influential or critical nodes? (centrality)
  • Are there distinct subgroups or factions? (community detection)
  • How connected is the network overall? (density, components)
  • What is the shortest path between two actors? (geodesic distance)
  • Does the network have a hierarchical or flat structure? (hierarchy index)


Vulnerability Questions

  • Which node or edge removal would maximally fragment the network?
  • Are there single points of failure (articulation points, bridges)?
  • How does the network respond to disruption? (robustness simulation)
  • Has the network adapted after a previous disruption?

Relational Questions

  • Who is the likely broker between otherwise disconnected groups?
  • Which actors occupy structurally equivalent positions?
  • Is there evidence of coordination or coincidence in timing of ties?
  • Who has disproportionate access to information flow?


Temporal Questions

  • How has the network evolved over time?
  • Is the network growing or contracting?
  • Did a specific event trigger network restructuring?
  • Are new nodes being recruited into the network?


Connecting to Course

Each of these question types maps to specific methods and tools covered in this course.

Data Sources for Intelligence Network Analysis

OSINT-Derived Network Data

  • Social media: follower/following graphs, interaction networks, co-hashtag networks
  • Corporate registries: beneficial ownership, director interlocks, subsidiary structures
  • Court records and indictments: named co-conspirators, financial transactions
  • News and event data: co-occurrence of actors in events, meetings, travel
  • Academic and professional networks: co-authorship, conference attendance
  • Leaked databases: Panama Papers, FinCEN Files, Pandora Papers

Classified / Controlled Source Data

  • SIGINT: communications metadata (who called whom, when, for how long)
  • HUMINT: reported relationships, organizational rosters
  • Financial intelligence: transaction records, account associations
  • Biometric and identity data: co-location, travel records
  • Law enforcement databases: known associates, gang rosters


Data Quality and Completeness

All network data in intelligence contexts is incomplete. Clandestine actors evade collection. Analysts must reason carefully about what is missing and how gaps affect structural conclusions.1

  1. Everton, Disrupting Dark Networks, 37–42.

The Course Arc: From Foundations to Intelligence Products

Where We Are Going

This course builds competency across three dimensions:

  1. Conceptual: Graph theory, centrality, community structure, temporal dynamics, multi-layer networks
  2. Technical: Gephi, i2 Analyst Notebook, ArcGIS, Python/NetworkX — each appropriate to different analytical tasks
  3. Applied: Domain-specific network types (social, financial, infrastructure, information, global security) with real-world datasets


The final project integrates all three: a network intelligence product on an analyst-selected topic, including written assessment and briefing.

Lecture Summary and Key Terms

Core Definitions

  • Graph \(G = (V, E)\): a set of nodes \(V\) and edges \(E\)
  • Node (vertex): entity in the network
  • Edge (link, tie): relationship between nodes
  • Directed graph: edges have direction (source \(\to\) target)
  • Weighted graph: edges carry numeric values
  • Bipartite graph: two node types; edges only between types
  • Density \(\Delta\): ratio of actual to possible edges
  • Dark network: covert, trust-based, illicit relational system

Key Takeaways

  1. Network analysis is a relational paradigm — structure matters as much as attributes
  2. The same mathematical framework applies across all domains: social, financial, infrastructure, information
  3. Density, directionality, and weight fundamentally change what a network tells you
  4. Dark networks are deliberately sparse; bridge nodes are highest-value targets
  5. Network analysis has real limitations: incomplete data and structural findings require interpretive judgment
